conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. You’re here for left pelvic pain that’s come back, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the same sharp pain I’ve had before. It came back three days ago and it’s been really bad. I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were in the ED earlier and got some pain meds. How are you feeling now compared to then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but still uncomfortable. The morphine helped a bit, but I’m worried it’ll get bad again at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to restart your regular pain medications like ibuprofen, gabapentin, and tramadol. The gynecology team reviewed your case and agrees this looks like another flare of your endometriosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But why did my lactate go up? I saw that in the notes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your lactate was slightly elevated at 3.3 when you arrived, which can happen with pain and dehydration. It improved to 2.4 after fluids and pain control, so we’re not concerned about infection or serious organ issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s a relief. I’ve been really nauseous and haven’t eaten much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV fluids to help with that. Once you can keep food down, we’ll switch to oral meds. You’re also on omeprazole for your reflux, which might help the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your labs from this morning. Your potassium is now 3.6, which is better, and your kidney function is normal. Your pain seems more stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’m feeling a little better. I had some toast and didn’t throw up. But my hemoglobin is down again, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin dropped from 11.9 to 9.9. You’ve had low iron before, and it’s likely related to your periods. We’re not starting iron now because it can make nausea worse, but your colonoscopy will help us check for other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, the colonoscopy is scheduled next week. I’m nervous about that. Do they think the endometriosis is in my bowel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why it’s important. Sometimes endometriosis can affect the rectum or bowel wall. The test will help the surgeons plan the best approach. It’s a key step before any surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my lithium level was checked? I’ve been feeling a bit flat lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your level is 0.7, which is in the normal range. Your TSH was high last time, possibly due to lithium, but you’re not showing signs of hypothyroidism, so no new meds are needed for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting ready to discharge you. Your pain is much improved, and you’re keeping food and meds down. You’ll go home on your usual medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I do if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using your prescribed pain meds as directed. If the pain becomes unmanageable, go to the Gynecology Triage clinic in the Women’s Health Building. They’ll see you quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up with gynecology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment next week, and your surgery will be planned after the colonoscopy. They’ll discuss laparoscopic fulguration once they know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I feel a lot more confident going home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your primary and gynecology teams have all the details. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I be worried about the anemia long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we’ll monitor. The colonoscopy will help rule out bleeding sources. For now, focus on managing your pain and nutrition. We’ll reassess after your tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, that helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications. Feel free to ask them any questions too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you again, Dr. Lee.
